newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Juppe defiant on party's 20th anniversary.
newsitem.headline: France's Juppe defiant on party's 20th anniversary.

text.p: France's fractious ruling party, the Gaullist Rally for the Republic (RPR), celebrated its 20th anniversary on Sunday with embattled Prime Minister Alain Juppe calling on critics to stop sniping and unite behind him.
"Shake off the blues," Juppe, president of the RPR, told two rallies of the conservative party founded by President Jacques Chirac as political heir to post-war leader General Charles de Gaulle.
Juppe called on the Gaullists to overcome differences and unite behind his austerity reforms to bring France into the European single currency in 1999.
Juppe, who was shaken by a crippling 12-day truckers' strike last month, said he bore no grudge against his Gaullist critics.
He spoke in Agen in his southwestern home region and later at a Paris rally.
"We have differences sometimes, even major differences ... but we also feel we belong to the same family and this is stronger than differences."

Juppe was buoyed by Chirac's support after a call by ex-president Valery Giscard d'Estaing for a depreciation of the franc to revive economic growth and combat record unemployment drew significant sympathy among RPR backbenchers.
Chirac, receiving German Chancellor Helmut Kohl on a visit to the southwestern town of Perigueux on Saturday, reaffirmed his commitment to a stable franc-mark parity.

Juppe indicated he was determined to press ahead with his reforms to cut the state deficit despite his growing unpopularity which has prompted his former Gaullist cabinet colleague Charles Pasqua to say that Chirac should reshuffle the cabinet or bring forward a general election scheduled in 1998.

"Gaullism is being able to say 'no' when everyone says 'yes'," Juppe said. "France's economy is being revived, its society is being modernised...The courage to carry out reforms will pay off, I am certain of it."
Addressing the Paris rally, Pasqua pledged loyalty to Chirac but renewed his anti-Maastricht rhetoric, saying: "The republic is neither a market nor a currency, much less a bank."
"We may associate with others for all of this, but we do not have to bow to all their conditions."
Juppe's Gaullist rival Philippe Seguin addressed a separate rally at Egletons, in the southwest, where Chirac 20 years ago founded the RPR as "a Labour movement a la Francaise".
"Anniversaries are intended not only for memories. They are to blaze a trail, to search for new paths, to renew," he said.

A former anti-Maastricht campaigner, Seguin, the National Assembly speaker, has been advocating greater emphasis on the fight against record unemployment. He has been mentioned as a possible successor to Juppe.

Socialist opposition leader Lionel Jospin seized on the anniversary to recall judicial probes underway into suspicion of illegal RPR financing and accuse the Gaullists of forfeiting de Gaulle's independence ideas by bringing France back into NATO.
"The RPR was made 20 years ago for a man. What remained of the Gaullist ideals has been undone," he told Europe 1 radio.
Chirac picked up the pieces of a crumbling Gaullist movement in 1976 to found the RPR after resigning as prime minister to the then centrist president Giscard d'Estaing.
He went on to be elected mayor of Paris in 1977 and build a political base that led the Gaullists to win the 1986 general election under the late Socialist president Francois Mitterrand.
Chirac was prime minister from 1986 to 1988. He handed over the presidency of the RPR to Juppe in 1994 and won the French presidency in May last year.
